Grace Southworth's people came north by the same road as the Hutchinses, a step at a time.
Constant Southworth, Governor Bradford's stepson, raised his family at Duxbury;
his son William settled at Little Compton, Rhode Island; William's son Nathaniel,
a ship carpenter, moved inland to Mansfield, Connecticut, about 1720, then sailed on a voyage to the Mediterranean
about 1730 and never came back. His son Constant spent his whole life at Mansfield,
town clerk for fifty years and a deacon, and his wife Mary Porter lived to 101.
After the Revolution the next Constant went north, first to Weybridge, Vermont,
where his son Francis was born in 1808, and then across Lake Champlain to Bangor,
in Franklin County, New York, where the town's Presbyterian church was organized in 1809 in his barn near Cook's Corners.
Francis farmed at Bangor until his death in 1875.
His son Moses, a farmer at Cook's Corners and an ordained preacher of the Christian Church there,
was the father of Grace, who married DeWitt Hutchins of Fort Covington.
The Briggses came the same way: Lieutenant Henry Briggs of Dighton, Massachusetts,
a soldier of 1775, ended his days at Westville, and his son Winchester, born in Vermont in 1797,
built a sawmill on the Deer River.
